paper_title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Reasoning language models answer with long chains of thought, often tens of thousands of tokens long. Each generated token requires reading all of the models weights from memory, so generation speed is capped by memory bandwidth rather than compute. Storing weights in two bits instead of bf16 reduces weight memory and the memory traffic per token by up to 8. Above three bits per weight, scalar quantization formats, which store one integer per weight and one scale per group of weights, are already close to lossless. At two bits, however, the strongest methods go beyond this format. They use vector codebooks, rotations, zero-points, or distillation-based quantization-aware training (QAT) with small groups [5, 13, 15, 45, 48]. Scalar formats remain the easiest to deploy, because dequantizing weight takes single multiplication. However, it is still an open question whether two-bit scalar format can preserve models ability to reason through difficult problems. Answering this question first requires fixing how two-bit models are evaluated. They are usually compared by perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy. These metrics barely separate configurations whose sampled reasoning accuracy differs by more than ten points (fig. 1b), because likelihood based metrics, score single-token predictions and never check whether long chain of thought eventually reaches correct answer. two-bit framework for reasoning models should therefore be both designed for and evaluated on reasoning tasks. We design such framework, ThinkBit, presented in fig. 1a) with one primary constraint in mind. The constraint is that we want strictly scalar quantization format. Every stored weight is an integer codeword multiplied by bf16 scale shared by group of 128 weights, with no vector codebooks, rotations, or zero-points. Our proposed framework has five stages. First, sensitivity-based bit allocation assigns precision to each layer. Second, block-wise codeword search chooses the initial codewords. Third, scale recalibration repairs the quantized model while leaving every codeword unchanged. Fourth, for even more flexibility, QAT reassigns the small number of codewords that still affect the output. Finally, paired reasoning test on MATH training problems decides whether to keep the QAT checkpoint (QAT) or the 1 recalibrated checkpoint (Rec). We compare both checkpoints against QAT-only baseline (QAT-only), which skips the bit allocation, codeword search and recalibration phases. (a) The proposed framework (ThinkBit), has five stages. (1) Kronecker-factored Hessian sensitivity (KronQ [34]) assigns each layer ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier. (2) GSQ [6] starts from layer-wise PTQ solution and searches for codewords. (3) Scale recalibration freezes the codewords and trains only the stored bfloat16 (bf16) scales and the root-mean-square normalization (RMSNorm) gains. (4) QAT reassigns codewords. (5) paired reasoning test on MATH training problems decides which checkpoint to keep. (b) Change in accuracy relative to the Qwen3-1.7B QAT checkpoint (QAT-hbf16; names in table 2). All variants use the same bf16 head and embedding. Removing codeword search, scale recalibration, or both keeps the 7-task mean in the range of 53.754.8, but lowers sampled MATH-500 accuracy from 43 to 35.0, 37.0, and 32.1 presented in table 8 (uniform 2-bit allocation instead of mixed tiers to 28.4). The recalibrated checkpoint without QAT (Rec-hbf16) is lower on the 7-task mean (51.5) but higher on reasoning (47.5). Standard benchmarks therefore dont detect losses in reasoning correctly and could misguide checkpoint selection. Figure 1: Overview of our 2-bit quantization framework ThinkBit and importance of different stages What 2-bit means. The label 2-bit does not by itself say how large model is. Community quantizations portrayed as 2-bit usually keep the embeddings, the output head, and other sensitive tensors at higher precision, so their real storage cost is well above two bits per parameter. For example, Unsloths 2-bit releases [75] in the GGUF file format of llama.cpp [21] store 2.82-3.62 bits per parameter for Qwen3-1.7B and 2.42-3.12 for Qwen3-14B. Similarly, PrismMLs ternary Bonsai model [55], whose weights need about log2 3 1.585 bits each, actually stores 2.15 bits per parameter for Qwen3-1.7B: every ternary weight sits in 2-bit slot, with one FP16 scale per 128 weights. Hence, comparing such models by their nominal bit-width can hide differences in size of up to 50%. We therefore compare models by whole-model size in bytes, counting every stored tensor. By this measure, our 0.52 GB Qwen3-1.7B checkpoint stores 2.42 bits per parameter including the output head and embeddings, which is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the same model. 2 Our work makes the following key contributions: Two-bit models must be selected on reasoning tasks On Qwen3-1.7B, removing the codeword search, scale recalibration, both, or the budget allocation stage keeps the 7-task QA task average at 53.7-54.8, within 1.5-point margin. However, skipping these stages lowers MATH-500 accuracy from 43.0 after QAT stage to the range of 28.437.0  (Table 8)  , showing that selecting two-bit models on reasoning tasks is crucial since that is where most of the degradations are seen. ThinkBit: novel scalar two-bit framework built for reasoning. We propose novel five stage framework (fig. 1a) (1) Allocate: Allocate precisions appropriately for each layer (2) Search: Search the integer codewords block by block (3) Recalibrate: Recalibrate the stored scales with the codewords frozen (4) QAT: Let quantizationaware training (QAT) reassign codewords and (5) Selection: Keep the better of the Stage-3 and Stage-4 checkpoints by reasoning test. On Qwen3-1.7B our framework reaches 47.5 on sampled MATH-500 before QAT and 43.0 after, against 18.524.1 and 32.637.8 from tuned GPTQ initializations  (Table 9)  . Better two-bit reasoning per byte. At matched size (about 0.5 GB), our recalibrated checkpoint (Rec-h2) scores 46.7 on MATH-500, against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data and tokens. At 0.52 GB, smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model, the selected checkpoint scores higher than all of them on MATH-500  (Table 7)  .

sections.title: 2 Methodology
sections.content: ThinkBit turns bf16 model into model whose linear-layer weights are stored as small integers. Stages 12 work layer by layer on calibration data; Stages 34 recover or train the whole model against the bf16 model; Stage 5 only evaluates. Algorithm 2 in section gives the full procedure and table 10 in the appendix summarizes the notation. All models use the same experimental settings and we focus mainly on the Qwen3 [80] model family in our experiments.

sections.content: Fine-tuning only the higher-precision parameters, the scales and the RMSNorm gains, is cheap since they make up less than 1% of the model (one scale per 128 weights) and hence the optimizer state stays small. sections.title: 3 Experimental setup
sections.content: Models. We primarily study ThinkBit on the Qwen-3 family. Specifically, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B and Qwen314B [80] (thinking mode, native tool calling; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B have untied heads). For all models we use the same hyperparameters for ThinkBit. Data. The quantization and training data mixture has three parts (i) each models own bf16 replies to prompts, namely Magicoder code instructions, GSM8K-train and MetaMathQA math problems, Hermes and Glaive tool calls, TriviaQA, Natural Questions and WebQuestions training questions, and MMLU-auxiliary questions without answers; (ii) the models own continuations of FineWeb-Edu and Wikipedia passages; and (iii) raw text from FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb, Wikipedia (WikiText articles removed), OpenWebMath, Evol-Instruct code, Hermes and Glaive multi-turn tool conversations and Python source (codeparrot-clean). Replies are sampled with each models chat template, which for Qwen3 includes the thinking block, and are capped at 4,096 tokens, so training never sees complete long reasoning trace. Table 3 lists the data and amount used by each stage. Reasoning data for the final QAT. The stage studies (sections 4 and 7) use the mixture above. The selected checkpoints of sections 5 and 6 repeat Stage 4 for longer on mixture that adds complete long reasoning traces: each models own bf16 thinking-mode answers to public math and code prompts and to hard competition problems (OpenMathReasoning and OpenCodeReasoning statements; truncated traces dropped), DeepSeek-R1 solutions from OpenMathReasoning, and PG-19 books and arXiv papers for long context; at 1.7B also OpenR1-Math-220k, Codeforces CoTs, OpenCodeReasoning, OpenCodeInstruct and Cosmopedia textbooks. Reasoning traces make up about 60% of the mixture. Every source passes the same decontamination against all evaluated benchmarks as the base mixture. At 1.7B, QAT+R-h2 starts from Rec-h2 (2.1B tokens, learning rate 2 103); at 8B and 14B it starts from further recalibration of Rec-h2 on the long-trace data (1.1B tokens, 1.5 103); format and bytes are unchanged. Checkpoint names. We name every checkpoint by the stages it went through  (table 2)  : base name for the codeword start and the trained stages, suffix for the precision of the head and embedding, and +R when Stage 4 (or 3) used the reasoning mixture. Selected marks the checkpoint kept by Stage 5. The same names are used in every table, caption and figure. Evaluation. Dense bf16 exports are scored with the Language Model Evaluation Harness (lm-eval) [20] and served by vLLM. The core suite contains ARC-e/c, MMLU, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA and LAMBADA; their mean log-likelihood accuracy is the 7-task mean. Generation covers math, code, instruction following and tool use on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [54]. The broad suite adds MMLU-Pro, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA, SciQ, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, BoolQ, RACE, Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark Hard (BBH), MATH-500, GSM8K chain-of-thought (GSM8K-CoT), Instruction Following Evaluation (IFEval), Mostly Basic Python Problems (MBPP) and HumanEval+. American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) 2024/2025 and MATH-500 use the models chat/thinking format; We report thinking-mode MATH-500 in two ways. Greedy decodes each problem once and grades it with lm-eval. Sampled draws four answers per problem (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, up to 32k new tokens) and scores them strictly: an answer counts only if the reasoning trace closes with </think> and the final answer is correct. sections.title: 4 Where does the quality come from?
sections.content: We follow Qwen3-1.7B through Stages 3 and 4 (table 4 and fig. 2) and then split reasoning accuracy into finishing trace and solving the problem  (table 5)  . Recalibration closes most of the likelihood gap. With the Stage 2 codewords frozen, recalibration lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 46.91 to 19.46 (bf16: 16.67), raises the 7-task mean from 43.8 to 51.5 (bf16: 58.9) and sampled MATH-500 from 14.8 to 47.5  (Table 4)  . The scales do almost all of the work: held-out KL is 0.641 after GSQ, 0.282 with the scales trained, 0.418 with only the RMSNorm gains trained and 0.282 with both (Table 19 in Section H). The scales fit the output, not the weights. Recalibration moves each scale by median of 6% (log-offset = 0.062 in = s0er, Section 2.4), but not toward the scale that best fits the frozen codewords in weight space, = Wg, cg/cg, cg for group g: rg has the same sign as log(s g/s0,g) in 51% of groups, and the two correlate at 0.07. Relative weight error c2/W 2 therefore improves slightly, from 0.386 to 0.393, while would lower it to 0.277. The objective explains why. Equation (15) scores the whole networks output, so it weights each weight error by the activations it meets and lets the scales of one layer offset rounding errors in others. Block outputs show the same pattern (Table 20 in Section H). Given the same bf16 input, recalibrated block is further from its bf16 output than before (mean relative error 0.094 vs. 0.079), and the hidden states of the recalibrated network are further from bf16 on average (0.28 vs. 0.21), yet next-token KL on WikiText-2 falls from 1.30 to 0.57. Recalibration does not make intermediate representations more faithful; it adjusts them so that the output distribution matches. QAT reassigns few codewords. Long running QAT reassigns 6.4% of the codewords (Figure 2c), each by single grid step toward its bf16 weight (Section J); initialization, not learning rate, decides how many move (section I). It brings WikiText-2 to 16.54, partly through Wikipedia in its training mix, the 7-task mean to 54.6 and MMLU from 44.4 to 49.9. Sampled MATH-500 is 73.0 against bf16s 91.2 at 1.7B, 92.2 against 96.9 at 8B and 94.8 against 97.5 at 14B, and the 7-task mean is 53.8 against 58.9, 65.8 against 70.7 and 69.9 against 74.3, while the checkpoints take 0.52, 2.08 and 3.74 GB instead of 3.44, 16.4 and 29.5 GB. sections.title: 6 Model size and inference
sections.content: Training checkpoints store codewords in 4-bit containers; we re-pack them at their true widths and decode them again to verify the stored bytes (section M). With 2-bit head and embedding, the Qwen3-1.7B QAT and recalibrated checkpoints (QAT-h2, Rec-h2) each measure 0.520 GB (2.42 bits per original parameter; 2.046 per quantized weight with scales), and the Qwen3-14B QAT-only and recalibrated checkpoints (QAT-only-h2, Rec-h2) 3.74 GB; all four decode bit-identically and load in stock transformers. With bf16 tied embedding the 1.7B checkpoint (QAT-hbf16) is 0.977 GB, 64% of it embedding. Served by vLLM directly from the 4-bit containers on one H100, the 8B and 14B checkpoints take 5.68 and 9.31 GiB of weight memory instead of 15.27 and 27.52 GiB for bf16, and decode 212 and 150 tokens/s at batch 1 instead of 146 and 86 (section M). Equal bytes, same harness. Table 7 and section compare our Qwen3-1.7B checkpoints with PrismMLs Bonsai releases [55], the official EfficientQAT and BitDistiller trained on our base mixture, and Unsloths llama.cpp quantizations [21, 75] of the same model, calibrated with an importance matrix, decoded to bf16 and scored with the same harness. sections.title: 8 Related work
sections.content: Post-training quantization of LLMs. The first LLM quantizers targeted 8-bit weights and activations, using finegrained quantization with layer-wise distillation (ZeroQuant [81]), mixed-precision decomposition of outlier features (LLM.int8() [7]) or rescaling that moves outliers from activations to weights (SmoothQuant [78]). For weight-only quantization, GPTQ [19] turns Optimal Brain Compression [18] into one-shot second-order rounding, AWQ [40] protects salient channels by rescaling, and SpQR [9] and SqueezeLLM [31] store sparse outlier weights at higher precision. Learned rounding and clipping optimize layer or block reconstruction (AdaRound [52], BRECQ [38], OmniQuant [57], CBQ [10], TesseraQ [37]). Most of these methods are close to lossless at three to four bits but degrade 17 sharply at two. GSQ [6], which we build on, learns each weights grid assignment and the group scales jointly through Gumbel-softmax relaxation of scalar grid. Two-bit and sub-two-bit formats. The strongest two-bit results leave the scalar format. Incoherence processing (QuIP [4]), combined with lattice or trellis codebooks (QuIP# [58], QTIP [59]), and additive vector quantization with fine-tuning (AQLM [15], PV-Tuning [48]) reach strong perplexity, and fixed or learned rotations (QuaRot [2], SpinQuant [44]) remove outliers so that weights, activations and the KV cache are easier to quantize. Binary and partially binarized quantization (BiLLM [24], PB-LLM [56]) reaches about one bit per weight at clear accuracy cost, while binary and ternary models trained from scratch (BitNet [76], BitNet b1.58 [46], Spectra [29]) show that very low-bit weights can be competitive when the pretraining budget allows. We keep strictly scalar format with one bf16 scale per group of 128 weights, which dequantizes with one multiplication and needs no codebook or rotation at inference; rotations are orthogonal to our stages and could be combined with them. Quantization-aware training and distillation. QAT trains through the rounding with straight-through estimators [3, 25] or learned step sizes [16]. For LLMs, LLM-QAT [43] distills from the full-precision model on self-generated data, BitDistiller [13] combines asymmetric quantization with self-distillation, EfficientQAT [5] trains all parameters block by block and then only the quantization step sizes end to end, OneBit [79] factors weights into signs and value vectors, and ParetoQ [45] compares 1to 4-bit QAT within one framework. Parameter-efficient methods train only scales, adapters or normalization layers on frozen low-bit weights (PEQA [30], QLoRA [8], norm tweaking [35]); our scale recalibration is closest to these, but fits scales and gains to the bf16 models output distribution with codewords frozen. Our recalibration and QAT distill with the forward KL to the bf16 model [23]; reverse-KL and on-policy distillation [1, 22] are alternatives we do not use. We show that, at fixed token budget, the post-training starting point and reasoning-based selector decide how much reasoning survives. Mixed precision and sensitivity. Since HAWQ, second-order sensitivity has guided bit allocation [11, 12]. KronQ [34] scores each layer with the activation and gradient traces of Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation (as in KFAC [49]); we use its score to choose ternary, 2-bit or 3-bit tiers under bit budget (section 2). Evaluating quantized models. Systematic evaluations find that perplexity can miss losses on knowledge-intensive tasks [26] and that quantization affects dialogue and long-context tasks differently from basic NLP tasks [36], although perplexity remains reasonable proxy on many standard benchmarks [28]; perplexity is also unreliable for long-context ability in general [17]. Matched accuracy can hide answer flips [14], and 8-bit and 4-bit weight-only formats are close to lossless across academic and real-world tasks [33]. Scaling studies relate the useful precision to model size and training tokens [32, 53]. For reasoning models, quantization below four bits hurts most on hard problems [42]; whether it lengthens traces is disputed, with no increase reported by Liu et al. [42] and token inflation at 3 and 4 bits by Lian et al. [39]. Qwen3 has been evaluated down to 1 bit with perplexity and zero-shot accuracy [83]; reasoning-specific quantizers use fine-tuning signals [82] or the models own reasoning traces as calibration data [77]; and budget forcing [51] controls how long model thinks. These studies compare quantized model with its full-precision parent. We use paired tests [50] to show that likelihood also fails to rank competing two-bit configurations, and select checkpoints on held-out reasoning problems instead.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose ThinkBit, strictly scalar two-bit quantization framework designed to preserve reasoning. ThinkBit allocates ternary, 2-bit or 3-bit tier to each layer by sensitivity, searches the integer codewords block by block, recalibrates the stored scales with the codewords frozen, lets quantization-aware training reassign codewords, and keeps the better checkpoint by paired reasoning test on training problems. Our main finding is that likelihood-based metrics hide what two-bit quantization does to reasoning: removing codeword search, scale recalibration or tier allocation barely changes the log-likelihood mean but clearly lowers sampled MATH-500, and selecting checkpoints by reasoning test, without touching the test set, picks the stronger model. Trained on the same data, our checkpoints reason better than EfficientQAT and BitDistiller at every size we compared. With reasoning traces in the final training stage, the selected checkpoints are smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the same model; they reason better than all of them at 1.7B, 18 match Q2_K at 8B and 14B at about two thirds of its size, and at 14B come within few points of bf16 on MATH-500. Files of four or more bits per parameter remain stronger, and some two-bit reasoning traces still do not finish. There are many potential directions for future work. First, kernels that read 2and 3-bit codewords directly would turn the smaller files into proportional memory and speed gains at inference time, which the 4-bit containers used here cannot show. Second, training objectives that reward finishing reasoning trace, such as on-policy distillation from the bf16 teacher or reinforcement learning after quantization, may close much of the remaining gap to bf16. Third, the stage study should be repeated on more model families, mixture-of-experts models and models above 14B, and the tier allocation could be extended below two bits. Finally, selectors for code and tool use would extend checkpoint selection beyond math problems. We will release the code upon acceptance.

sections.title: E Further ablations
sections.content: This section details the controls of section 7. Table 14 compares codeword search with stronger GPTQ starts, table 15 collects the remaining paired contrasts, and table 16 tests equivalence on the 7-task suite. Unless noted, reasoning is sampled, strictly scored MATH-500 with paired tests. Rounding-only alternatives to QAT. Moving codewords toward their bf16 values without training, then briefly recalibrating the scales, is worse than not moving them (re-round rows of table 8). GSQs non-nearest codewords therefore beat nearest rounding; these short controls do not separate QATs choice of codewords from its longer optimization. Scales, gains and reverted reassignments. Recalibrating the scales alone matches recalibrating scales and gains, while the gains alone recover much less (tables 8 and 19). Reverting QATs MLP reassignments lowers MMLU but raises HumanEval, and reverting its attention reassignments lowers GSM8K  (table 8)  . These are interventions on single checkpoint. 28 Initialization and the reassigned codewords. Latents that start on their codewords (α=0) are almost never reassigned, at either learning rate (section I). With α=0.5 the reassignments are single grid steps toward the bf16 weight, concentrated in value projections and the 3-bit tier (section J); their direction largely follows from eq. (17), which starts each latent on the side of its codeword where the bf16 weight lies. Rules with likelihood conjunct. Two likelihood rules, written before the reasoning results, would have removed stages that the paired reasoning tests show are needed. Codeword search was to stay only if the layer-wise start lost at least 3 MMLU and 5 thinking-math points; the MMLU gap is 1.2, so the rule drops the search. Recalibration was to stay if skipping it cost more than one MMLU point; it costs 1.03, boundary case. Stronger starts. To test whether codeword search only beats weak start, two starts replace the layer-wise one with the same tier map: GPTQ on every tier with MSE-clipped scales, and the same followed by Hessian-weighted Gumbel rounding. Each then receives the same recalibration and QAT. After recalibration their perplexities are close to ours, but their reasoning is more than 20 points lower; QAT narrows the gap without closing it, while the likelihood and code columns barely separate the three (table 14; paired tests in table 9). sections.title: I QAT initialization and learning rate
sections.content: Figure 6 crosses the latent initialization α of eq. (17) with the learning rate. Latents that start on their codewords (α=0) almost never cross rounding boundary at either learning rate. With α=0.5, KL first rises while codewords are reassigned and then falls below its starting value. Figure 6: QAT latent initialization α learning rate on Qwen3-1.7B (short runs from the recalibrated model). (a) Heldout KL relative to the start. (b) Share of codewords changed. With α = 0 fewer than 0.003% of codewords are reassigned. Validation sequences are the chunks that follow each runs training slice, so runs with different training lengths are scored on different held-out text; this is why the starting KL (0.251) differs from long QATs (0.311). KL values are comparable within run, not across runs.

sections.title: J Where QAT reassigns codewords
sections.content: QAT reassigns 6.4% of the codewords. Figure 7 shows that the reassignments concentrate in value projections, the 3-bit tier and the last block, and that the reassigned codewords are mostly those already more than half grid step from their bf16 value; almost every reassignment is single step toward that value. 32 Figure 7: Where long QAT reassigns codewords on Qwen3-1.7B. (b) Share changed in each transformer block, with the share per tier in the inset text. The dotted line at 0.5 is the rounding boundary: most reassigned codewords lie beyond it, and 99.8% of reassignments move one step toward the bf16 weight.
